opus-5.5.text:
That's a connection I've thought about quite a bit. When we did ResNeXt, the core idea was what we called "cardinality": instead of making a network deeper or wider, you split a block into many parallel paths with the same topology and aggregate them. The surprising finding on ImageNet was that increasing cardinality, the number of these parallel transformations, was a more effective way to improve accuracy than just going deeper or wider, at roughly the same compute and parameter budget. Under a fixed FLOP budget, it's a better way to spend capacity.

Looking back, I'd say ResNeXt and MoE share an intuition, but they differ in an important way. Both say you don't need one monolithic transformation. You can decompose the computation into many smaller "experts," or branches, and that decomposition is a powerful axis for scaling. In ResNeXt we used grouped convolution, so every branch is always active. It's a dense split-transform-merge. MoE takes the next step and asks: what if you don't activate all branches for every input? What if you route? That's where the real scaling leverage comes from, because you decouple total parameter count from per-token compute.

So in a sense, ResNeXt was "dense MoE" without a router. We showed that cardinality is a useful dimension. MoE showed that if you make it conditional, you can push that dimension much further, to hundreds of experts or more, without paying proportionally in FLOPs.

There's also a lesson I think carries over. The reason ResNeXt worked well wasn't only the multi-branch idea. It was that we kept the design extremely simple and homogeneous: every branch has the same shape, and you have one hyperparameter to tune. Earlier multi-branch designs, like Inception, were hand-crafted and hard to scale. I see a similar tension in MoE today. The most successful MoE designs tend to be the ones that are simple and regular, like fine-grained experts with uniform structure, rather than very heterogeneous, hand-engineered routing schemes. Simplicity is what lets something scale.

What's different now is the bottleneck. In the ImageNet era, the question was mostly accuracy per FLOP. In the LLM era, with MoE, a lot of the hard problems are systems problems: load balancing, communication across devices, memory bandwidth, and training stability of the router. ResNeXt never had to deal with those, because grouped convolution lives on one device and has no routing decisions to go wrong.

And personally, I find it interesting that in vision we haven't fully exploited MoE-style conditional computation yet, at least not the way language models have. Visual tokens are very redundant, and there's a natural argument that conditional computation should be even more useful there. So I sometimes feel the idea started in vision, matured in language, and may eventually come back to vision in a more powerful form.

r001.rationale: It says increasing cardinality improved ImageNet accuracy at roughly the same compute and explicitly describes it as a better use of capacity under a fixed FLOP budget.

r002.rationale: It connects ResNeXt’s dense, always-active branches to MoE’s expert decomposition, but explicitly distinguishes that from MoE’s conditional routing. It does not say ResNeXt scaled through increased sparsity at fixed compute.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I'll be honest, when we did ResNeXt back in 2016, nobody was thinking about mixture-of-experts. The motivation was much simpler. We had ResNet, we had Inception, and Inception had this split-transform-merge idea that clearly worked but was incredibly hand-designed. Every stage had different branch widths, different kernel sizes, and you couldn't scale it without redesigning it. So the question we asked was, can we take the "split" idea and make it homogeneous, make it a single knob you can turn?

That knob became cardinality, the number of parallel branches. And the interesting empirical finding on ImageNet was that if you hold FLOPs and parameters fixed, increasing cardinality gave you better accuracy than going deeper or going wider. Depth saturates, width saturates, but more branches kept giving you gains. That's really a statement about how you partition capacity, not about how much capacity you have.

Now, if you look at MoE through that lens, I think the connection is pretty direct. A ResNeXt block is essentially a dense mixture of experts where every expert is always on and the "router" is just a uniform sum. Grouped convolution is the implementation trick, but conceptually it's many small transforms operating on subspaces and then aggregated. MoE takes exactly that structure and adds a learned sparse gate, so you only activate a few branches per token. So in a sense, ResNeXt was the dense limit of MoE, and MoE is the sparse limit of ResNeXt.

The scaling story is where the parallel gets more nuanced. In ResNeXt we found that for fixed compute, the way you split matters a lot. MoE pushes this further: now parameters and compute are decoupled, so you can have a huge parameter count with modest active compute. But the design questions are the same ones we struggled with ten years ago. How many experts? How wide should each one be? Does the gain come from the experts really specializing, or is it mostly a form of regularization and ensembling? Back then, we actually had some evidence that the branches weren't doing anything semantically interpretable, they were just a better-conditioned way to spend the same parameters. I suspect a lot of the MoE story is similar, and a lot of the "expert specialization" narratives are a bit romanticized.

The other thing I'd point to is the lesson about simplicity. ResNeXt worked because the design had basically one hyperparameter. The MoE systems that scale well today also tend to converge to simple, homogeneous recipes, uniform experts, simple top-k routing, load balancing that's as light as possible. The complicated routing schemes mostly get thrown away. So the meta-lesson from ImageNet-era architecture research carries over: find the one axis that scales cleanly, make everything else boring, and let the data decide.

If anything, what's changed is that the bottleneck moved. In 2016 the constraint was FLOPs on a GPU for a single forward pass. Now it's memory bandwidth, communication across devices, and how you route tokens across chips. So the same architectural idea, split and aggregate, is being optimized for a completely different hardware cost model. I think that's actually the most interesting part. The idea stayed the same, the system around it changed, and that changed what "good scaling" even means.

r001.rationale: It says that, with FLOPs and parameters fixed, increasing ResNeXt cardinality (the number of parallel branches) improved ImageNet accuracy.

r002.rationale: It connects ResNeXt’s branch scaling to MoE, but describes ResNeXt as dense, with every branch active. It does not say ResNeXt scaled through increased sparsity at fixed compute.

astra-6.text:
I think the connection is the idea that you can scale a network along an axis other than depth or width. With ResNeXt, we called that axis cardinality—the number of parallel transformations. On ImageNet, increasing cardinality gave us a useful way to improve accuracy under a comparable computation budget.

That’s related to the motivation behind mixture-of-experts models: instead of making one transformation bigger, you build a collection of transformations. But there’s an important distinction. ResNeXt is dense: every branch participates for every input, and their outputs are aggregated. In a sparse MoE, a router selects which experts participate, so total parameter capacity can grow without increasing computation per token proportionally.

So I’d see ResNeXt as evidence that the organization of capacity matters, rather than as direct evidence for sparse expert scaling. MoE adds the question of conditional computation: how do you choose the experts, train the routing, and keep them effectively utilized? The shared intuition is that depth and width aren’t the only useful scaling dimensions. The mechanisms—and the challenges—are different.

r001.rationale: It says increasing ResNeXt cardinality improved ImageNet accuracy under a comparable computation budget; it defines cardinality as the number of parallel transformations.

r002.rationale: It draws a broad parallel between ResNeXt cardinality and MoE, but describes ResNeXt as dense and does not say its scaling came from increased sparsity at fixed compute.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the connection is this idea of cardinality—having multiple parallel transformations, rather than only making a network deeper or wider. In ResNeXt, we found that increasing cardinality was an effective way to improve ImageNet accuracy under a comparable complexity budget. So it suggested that the number of branches was a useful scaling dimension in its own right.

But there’s an important distinction: ResNeXt is dense. Every branch participates for every input. In a sparse MoE, a router selects a subset of experts, so you can increase total parameter capacity without increasing computation per token proportionally. That conditional computation is a substantial additional ingredient.

So I see a conceptual connection, rather than a direct equivalence. Both ask how to organize capacity across multiple transformations. ResNeXt explored that through a simple, homogeneous architecture; current MoE research adds the question of how to allocate computation dynamically. And that introduces challenges—routing, load balancing, communication—that the ImageNet results alone don’t answer.

r001.rationale: It says increasing cardinality improved ImageNet accuracy under a “comparable complexity budget,” but does not clearly state that the budget was fixed in FLOPs.

r002.rationale: It draws a conceptual connection to MoE, but describes ResNeXt as dense and does not say its scaling came from increased sparsity at fixed compute.
